title: Oaths & Interjections
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 50; Ryding Ch. 16, Ch. 37)
objectives: Identify oath particles (وَاوُ القَسَمِ, تَاءُ القَسَمِ, بَاءُ القَسَمِ) governing the genitive case.
Parse vocative constructions (يَا, أَيُّهَا / أَيَّتُهَا) across singular, muḍāf, and definite nouns.
recallPrompt: From Chapter 47: Which case do prepositions and oath particles govern?

sections.heading: Classical Oaths & Vocatives
sections.body: Classical prose and the Qur'an frequently open statements with oath particles (وَ, تَـ, بِـ — 'by...'), all of which are prepositions governing the genitive case. Separately, the vocative particle يَا ('O...') governs nouns in either a nominative-like invariable form (single definite/addressed noun) or the accusative (when annexed as muḍāf).

sections.label: Oath Governance & Vocative Rules
sections.summary: 1) Oath particles وَ, تَـ (restricted to اللَّهِ), and بِـ govern the sworn object in the GENITIVE (وَالعَصْرِ, تَاللَّهِ, وَاللَّهِ). 2) After يَا: a single addressed name takes single ḍammah without tanwīn (يَا زَيْدُ); an annexed muḍāf takes ACCUSATIVE (يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ); a noun with the definite article الـ requires أَيُّهَا / أَيَّتُهَا (يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ).

sections.heading: Oaths & Vocatives
rows: Genitive; تَـ used only with اللَّهِ

sections.irab: يَا: حَرْفُ نِدَاءٍ | طَالِبَ: مُنَادًى مُضَافٌ مَنْصُوبٌ بِالفَتْحَةِ | العِلْمِ: مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ مَجْرُورٌ
sections.notes: Because طَالِبَ is muḍāf, it takes accusative fatḥah after يَا.

sections.heading: Lām of the Oath Complement
sections.body: Affirmative statements answering an oath are typically introduced by لَـ or إِنَّ / لَقَدْ (e.g., وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ صَدَقَ).
